Lesson 10 · Decide where to expand

What happened as the rollout expanded?

We have evaluated a randomized pilot and a voluntary cohort. The final study follows another set of stores as the policy expands, using their earlier outcomes to construct the comparison.

Later rollout · S101–S150 · starts in week 25

Method in this decision: Difference-in-differences

The decision brief

The chain introduces alerts at 25 of the 50 remaining stores in week 25. These adopters were selected for high baseline stockout rates, so their starting levels differ from the comparison stores. The director asks what improved beyond the movement already occurring across the network. We will calculate each group’s change, compare those changes, and carry the result into the final spending recommendation.

Follow the same stores across the rollout date

This cohort consists of S101–S150. None received alerts before week 25. The before window is weeks 17–24, and the after window is weeks 25–32. Average each window within each store so that a store contributes one before value, one after value, and one change.

The selection rule gave alerts to stores with higher baseline rates. The comparison therefore focuses on movement rather than requiring identical starting levels. Review the implementation timeline with store teams: which week the service began and whether other operational changes happened alongside it.

Reconstruct the result from four averages

The before-and-after calculation
GroupBefore rate (%)After rate (%)After − before (points)
Later adopters13.7310.39-3.35
Comparison stores10.3611.601.24

First calculate the movement in each group. Then subtract the adopters’ change from the comparison change to report a positive number for a stockout reduction. The conventional difference-in-differences coefficient uses the reverse sign because it reports the change in the outcome rather than the reduction.

Estimated reduction = 1.24 − (-3.35) = 4.59 percentage points

Another way to see the calculation is to add the comparison change to the adopters’ starting rate. That gives a no-rollout benchmark of 14.97%. The actual adopter after-rate is 10.39%; the gap is the same 4.59-point reduction.

Connect the time comparison to the operating history

The design uses the comparison stores’ movement as the change adopters would have experienced under usual operations. In this case, the shared time pattern supplies that basis, while the stores retain different persistent levels. The pre-rollout chart and the operations timeline help make that comparison intelligible.

The 95% interval for the reduction is 3.92–5.25 points. It comes from variation across store-level changes, keeping all repeated weeks for a store together. The estimated accounting saving is 18.52 CU per adopter-week, with interval 12.91–24.13.

This cohort was selected differently from the pilot and the voluntary group. Its estimate answers a question about the later adopters. Compare the studies by their populations and designs before interpreting differences in their numerical results.

Complete a staged expansion recommendation

For stores resembling this later adopter group, the measured improvement and the cost rule support continuing a staged rollout. Preserve the implementation dates, store IDs, and monitoring basket so that the next phase can be evaluated in the same way.

The final memo should bring together the baseline burden, the forecast procedure, the randomized pilot, the voluntary comparison, and this rollout study. Give each estimate its own population and time window. Do not average the studies into one number without first defining the population that number would represent.

The synthesis page assembles those entries into a board-ready recommendation. The course ends with a decision whose evidence can be traced back through familiar rows and calculations.

Update the decision memo

For the later adopters, the time comparison estimates a 4.59-point reduction and 18.52 CU per store-week in accounting savings. Continue staged expansion for comparable stores, using the same outcome, cost rule, and recorded rollout dates.

Make the call

Why is the adopter group’s before-and-after improvement different from the reported policy reduction?

Compare your reasoning

Comparison stores also changed over the same period. Subtracting their movement constructs the benchmark for what adopters would have experienced without the rollout.

The bigger picture

Business outcomes move over time even when a new policy is introduced. Comparing changes gives the director a way to separate the wider movement from the rollout contrast. Across the course, the recurring work is to define the decision, identify the relevant comparison, calculate it transparently, and update the action.

After your decision: open the known answer

The shared world’s expected reduction among the later adopters is 4.47 points. The time-comparison estimate is 4.59, reflecting the observed product-day outcomes in this realization.
